claim: ICP34.5 can act as an antagonistic factor for the reactivation of HIV latency by herpes simplex virus type I (HSV-1).
source: We herein found that ICP34.5 can act as an antagonistic factor for the reactivation of HIV latency by herpes simplex virus type I (HSV-1), and thus recombinant HSV-1 with ICP34.5 deletion could more effectively reactivate HIV latency than its wild-type counterpart.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing differential reactivation effects between HSV-1 with and without ICP34.5 deletion.

claim: Recombinant HSV-1 with ICP34.5 deletion could more effectively reactivate HIV latency than its wild-type counterpart.
source: We herein found that ICP34.5 can act as an antagonistic factor for the reactivation of HIV latency by herpes simplex virus type I (HSV-1), and thus recombinant HSV-1 with ICP34.5 deletion could more effectively reactivate HIV latency than its wild-type counterpart.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C, 1E, and 1F comparing HSV-ΔICP34.5 to HSV-GFP.

claim: HSV-ΔICP34.5 promoted the phosphorylation of HSF1 by decreasing the recruitment of protein phosphatase 1 (PP1α).
source: Mechanistically, HSV-ΔICP34.5 promoted the phosphorylation of HSF1 by decreasing the recruitment of protein phosphatase 1 (PP1α), thus effectively binding to the HIV LTR to reactivate the latent reservoirs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including Co-IP assays and western blots shown in Figure 2.

claim: HSF1 effectively binds to the HIV LTR to reactivate the latent reservoirs.
source: Mechanistically, HSV-ΔICP34.5 promoted the phosphorylation of HSF1 by decreasing the recruitment of protein phosphatase 1 (PP1α), thus effectively binding to the HIV LTR to reactivate the latent reservoirs.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F demonstrating HSF1 binding to LTR.

claim: HSV-ΔICP34.5 enhanced the phosphorylation of IKKα/β through the degradation of IκBα.
source: In addition, HSV-ΔICP34.5 enhanced the phosphorylation of IKKα/β through the degradation of IκBα, leading to p65 accumulation in the nucleus to elicit NF-κB pathway-dependent reactivation of HIV latency.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HSV-ΔICP34.5 leads to p65 accumulation in the nucleus to elicit NF-κB pathway-dependent reactivation of HIV latency.
source: In addition, HSV-ΔICP34.5 enhanced the phosphorylation of IKKα/β through the degradation of IκBα, leading to p65 accumulation in the nucleus to elicit NF-κB pathway-dependent reactivation of HIV latency.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing nuclear p65 accumulation in Figure 2A.

claim: Recombinant HSV-ΔICP34.5 expressing SIV antigens effectively elicited SIV-specific immune responses in mice.
source: Results showed that these constructs effectively elicited SIV-specific immune responses, reactivated SIV latency, and delayed viral rebound after the interruption of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in chronically SIV-infected rhesus macaques.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISpot and ICS assay data shown in Figure 3F-M.

claim: Recombinant HSV-ΔICP34.5 expressing SIV antigens reactivated SIV latency in chronically SIV-infected rhesus macaques.
source: Results showed that these constructs effectively elicited SIV-specific immune responses, reactivated SIV latency, and delayed viral rebound after the interruption of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in chronically SIV-infected rhesus macaques.
evidence: This claim is supported by data on SIV Pol-specific immune responses and viral DNA measurements shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: Recombinant HSV-ΔICP34.5 expressing SIV antigens delayed viral rebound after the interruption of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in chronically SIV-infected rhesus macaques.
source: Results showed that these constructs effectively elicited SIV-specific immune responses, reactivated SIV latency, and delayed viral rebound after the interruption of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in chronically SIV-infected rhesus macaques.
evidence: This claim is supported by viral load monitoring data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Approximately 39.9 million people were living with HIV-1 as of 2023.
source: The epidemic of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), caused by human immunodeficiency virus type I (HIV-1), is still a huge challenge for global public health, with approximately 39.9 million people living with HIV-1 as of 2023.
evidence: This claim is based on established epidemiological data cited in the introduction.

claim: There is neither a curable drug nor a prophylactic vaccine for clinical use against HIV-1 infections.
source: To date, there is neither a curable drug nor a prophylactic vaccine for clinical use against HIV-1 infections (Sun et al., 2023b; Sun et al., 2023a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) can effectively control HIV-1 replication to an undetectable level.
source: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) can effectively control HIV-1 replication to an undetectable level, but the termination of ART usually results in prompt viral rebound from latent viral reservoirs (Archin et al., 2014; Looker et al., 2017; Calistri et al., 2003; Heng et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The termination of ART usually results in prompt viral rebound from latent viral reservoirs.
source: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) can effectively control HIV-1 replication to an undetectable level, but the termination of ART usually results in prompt viral rebound from latent viral reservoirs (Archin et al., 2014; Looker et al., 2017; Calistri et al., 2003; Heng et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by data in this study shown in Figure 5.

claim: The 'shock and kill' strategy is considered a promising approach for purging HIV-1 reservoirs.
source: The 'shock and kill' strategy is considered a promising approach for purging HIV-1 reservoirs, involving the activation of latently infected cells to express viral products (shock), followed by viral cytopathic effects or specific cytolytic T lymphocytes (CTLs) to eliminate the activated cells (kill) (Wu et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) features a 152 kb double-stranded DNA genome encoding over 80 proteins.
source: Herpes simplex virus (HSV), a human herpesvirus, features a 152 kb double-stranded DNA genome encoding over 80 proteins (Poh, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC), an HSV-1 variant with ICP34.5 deletion and GM-CSF insertion, received FDA approval in 2015 for treating malignant melanoma.
source: For example, talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC), an HSV-1 variant with ICP34.5 deletion and GM-CSF insertion, received FDA approval in 2015 for treating malignant melanoma, showcasing notable safety and efficacy in clinical practice.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about FDA-approved therapies.

claim: Prophylactic vaccines based on HSV, expressing simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) antigens, could elicit robust antigen-specific CTL responses in mice and monkeys.
source: Early studies indicated that prophylactic vaccines based on HSV, expressing simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) antigens, could elicit robust antigen-specific CTL responses in mice and monkeys, providing enduring and partial protection against pathogenic SIVmac239 challenges (Kaur et al., 2007; Murphy et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Prophylactic vaccines based on HSV expressing SIV antigens provided enduring and partial protection against pathogenic SIVmac239 challenges.
source: Early studies indicated that prophylactic vaccines based on HSV, expressing simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) antigens, could elicit robust antigen-specific CTL responses in mice and monkeys, providing enduring and partial protection against pathogenic SIVmac239 challenges (Kaur et al., 2007; Murphy et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HIV-specific CTL plays a crucial role in controlling viral replication and eliminating potential HIV reservoirs.
source: Moreover, increasing data suggest the crucial role of HIV-specific CTL in controlling viral replication and eliminating potential HIV reservoirs (Collins et al., 2020; Leitman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HSV infection in HIV patients is associated with increased HIV-1 viral load and disease progression.
source: Significantly, epidemiological research suggests a synergistic effect between HSV and HIV infections, with HSV infection in HIV patients being associated with increased HIV-1 viral load and disease progression (Looker et al., 2017; Calistri et al., 2003; Heng et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous epidemiological research.

claim: HSV can activate HIV latent reservoirs.
source: Some studies have further unveiled the ability of HSV to activate HIV latent reservoirs (Amici et al., 2004; Amici et al., 2001; Pierce et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Wild-type HSV-1 Mckrae strain can reactivate latent HIV in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Flow cytometry analysis showed a dose-dependent increase in green fluorescent protein (GFP) expression (Figure 1A), indicating that HSV-1 can reactivate latent HIV.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The attenuated HSV-1 strain can reactivate latent HIV at different MOIs.
source: Subsequently, we infected J-Lat 10.6 cells with an HSV-1 17 strain containing GFP (HSV-GFP) and observed a significant upregulation in the mRNA levels of HIV-1-driven transcripts, including Tat, Gag, Vif, and Vpr, along with 5'-LTR-containing RNA. This demonstrates that the attenuated HSV-1 strain can reactivate latent HIV at different MOIs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The mRNA levels of HIV-1 transcripts were significantly higher in J-Lat 10.6 cells infected with HSV-ΔICP34.5 compared to those treated with HSV-GFP.
source: Specifically, the mRNA levels of HIV-1 transcripts, including those driven by the 5' LTR, as well as Tat, Gag, Vpr, Vif were significantly higher in J-Lat 10.6 cells infected with HSV-ΔICP34.5 compared to those treated with HSV-GFP (Figure 1C), despite the weaker replication ability of HSV-ΔICP34.5 in these cells, as indicated by the mRNA level of HSV UL27 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HSV-ΔICP34.5 has weaker replication ability in J-Lat 10.6 cells compared to HSV-GFP.
source: Specifically, the mRNA levels of HIV-1 transcripts, including those driven by the 5' LTR, as well as Tat, Gag, Vpr, Vif were significantly higher in J-Lat 10.6 cells infected with HSV-ΔICP34.5 compared to those treated with HSV-GFP (Figure 1C), despite the weaker replication ability of HSV-ΔICP34.5 in these cells, as indicated by the mRNA level of HSV UL27 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1D and viral titer data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significantly higher level of p24 protein was found in the HSV-∆ICP34.5-infected ACH-2 cells compared to HSV-GFP-treated cells.
source: A significantly higher level of p24 protein, a key indicator of HIV replication, was found in the HSV-∆ICP34.5-infected ACH-2 cells compared to HSV-GFP-treated cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: HSV-ΔICP34.5 displayed a reduced capacity to reverse HIV latency in J-Lat 10.6-ICP34.5 cells compared to J-Lat 10.6 cells.
source: Our research revealed that HSV-ΔICP34.5 displayed a reduced capacity to reverse HIV latency in J-Lat 10.6-ICP34.5 cells compared to J-Lat 10.6 cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In J-Lat 10.6-ICP34.5 cells, the potency of latent reversal agents such as PMA and TNF-α was notably reduced when contrasted with J-Lat 10.6 cells.
source: Moreover, in J-Lat 10.6-ICP34.5 cells, the potency of latent reversal agents such as phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) and TNF-α was notably reduced when contrasted with J-Lat 10.6 cells (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: HSV-ΔICP34.5 induced a lower level of inflammatory cytokines (including IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α) in primary CD4+ T cells from PLWH compared to HSV-GFP stimulation.
source: In addition, HSV-ΔICP34.5 induced a lower level of inflammatory cytokines (including IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α) in primary CD4+ T cells from PLWH compared to HSV-GFP stimulation, likely due to its lower virulence and replication ability (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1I-K.

claim: Neither adenovirus nor vaccinia virus was able to reactivate HIV latency.
source: In addition, neither adenovirus nor vaccinia virus was able to reactivate HIV latency in this study (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and the deletion of ICP0 gene from HSV-1 diminished its reactivation effect on HIV latency (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The deletion of ICP0 gene from HSV-1 diminished its reactivation effect on HIV latency.
source: In addition, neither adenovirus nor vaccinia virus was able to reactivate HIV latency in this study (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and the deletion of ICP0 gene from HSV-1 diminished its reactivation effect on HIV latency (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Overexpressing ICP0 greatly reactivates latent HIV.
source: Importantly, overexpressing ICP0 greatly reactivates latent HIV (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), implying that this reactivation is virus-specific and that ICP0 plays an important role in reversing HIV latency.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: ICP0 plays an important role in reversing HIV latency.
source: Importantly, overexpressing ICP0 greatly reactivates latent HIV (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), implying that this reactivation is virus-specific and that ICP0 plays an important role in reversing HIV latency.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing ICP0 overexpression effects.

claim: HSV-ΔICP34.5 significantly enhanced the phosphorylation of IKKα/β.
source: J-Lat 10.6 cells were infected with HSV-GFP or HSV-ΔICP34.5, and results showed that HSV-ΔICP34.5 significantly enhanced the phosphorylation of IKKα/β, promoted the degradation of IKBα, and thus led to the accumulation of p65 in the nucleus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HSV-ΔICP34.5 promoted the degradation of IKBα.
source: J-Lat 10.6 cells were infected with HSV-GFP or HSV-ΔICP34.5, and results showed that HSV-ΔICP34.5 significantly enhanced the phosphorylation of IKKα/β, promoted the degradation of IKBα, and thus led to the accumulation of p65 in the nucleus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ICP34.5 protein had a specific interaction with IKKα/β.
source: Using the co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assay, we verified that the ICP34.5 protein had a specific interaction with IKKα/β, and then ICP34.5 could dephosphorylate IKKα/β.
evidence: This claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ICP34.5 could dephosphorylate IKKα/β.
source: Using the co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assay, we verified that the ICP34.5 protein had a specific interaction with IKKα/β, and then ICP34.5 could dephosphorylate IKKα/β.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the interaction data and the observed effects on phosphorylation.

claim: The overexpression of ICP34.5 effectively inhibited lipopolysaccharide-induced NF-κB pathway activation by inhibiting p65 entry into the nucleus.
source: Moreover, the overexpression of ICP34.5 effectively inhibited lipopolysaccharide-induced NF-κB pathway activation by inhibiting p65 entry into the nucleus (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The reactivation ability of HSV-ΔICP34.5 was significantly inhibited by KRIBB11 treatment in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The results indicated that the reactivation ability of HSV-ΔICP34.5 was significantly inhibited by KRIBB11 treatment in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: A significant enhancement of the binding of HSF1 to the HIV LTR was observed upon HSV-∆ICP34.5 infection.
source: Furthermore, a significant enhancement of the binding of HSF1 to the HIV LTR was observed upon HSV-∆ICP34.5 infection, leading to an increase in the reactivation of HIV latency (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: HSF1 was effectively dephosphorylated at Ser320 as a result of the overexpression of ICP34.5.
source: Importantly, HSF1 was effectively dephosphorylated at Ser320 as a result of the overexpression of ICP34.5, while no influence on the level of HSF1 expression was observed (Figure 2G and H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: A direct interaction between PP1α and HSF1 was found, allowing for the dephosphorylation of HSF1.
source: Additionally, a direct interaction between PP1α and HSF1 was found, allowing for the dephosphorylation of HSF1 and then affecting its ability to reactivate HIV latency (Figure 2J–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The frequency of SIV Gag-specific IFN-γ-secreting spot-forming cells (SFCs) in the HSV-sPD1-SIVgag group (1350 SFCs per 106 splenocytes) was significantly higher than that in the HSV-SIVgag group (498 SFCs per 106 splenocytes).
source: Of note, the frequency of SIV Gag-specific IFN-γ -secreting spot-forming cells (SFCs) in the HSV-sPD1-SIVgag group (1350 SFCs per 106 splenocytes) was significantly higher than that in the HSV-SIVgag group (498 SFCs per 106 splenocytes) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISpot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The frequency of SIV Env2-specific IFN-γ-secreting SFCs in the HSV-SIVenv group was significantly higher than the HSV-empty group.
source: The frequency of SIV Env2-specific IFN-γ -secreting SFCs in the HSV- SIVenv group was significantly higher than the HSV-empty group (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISpot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A heightened proportion of Gag-specific effector memory T cells (Tem) of CD8+ T cell subset in HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag group was observed in comparison to the HSV-Gag group.
source: Notably, a heightened proportion of Gag-specific effector memory T cells (Tem) of CD8+ T cell subset in HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag group was observed in comparison to the HSV-Gag group (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The blockade of PD1/PDL1 signaling pathway effectively enhanced vaccine-induced T cell immune responses.
source: Moreover, the blockade of PD1/PDL1 signaling pathway effectively enhanced vaccine-induced T cell immune responses, which was consistent with our and other previous studies (Zhou et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2022; Pan et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in this study and citations to previous literature.

claim: SIV Gag-specific ΔSFCs in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv group were greatly increased when compared with those in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-empty group and ART+saline group.
source: The results showed that SIV Gag-specific ΔSFCs in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv group were greatly increased when compared with those in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-empty group and ART+saline group (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISpot data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Plasma VL in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-empty group and the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv group exhibited a delayed rebound interval.
source: However, plasma VL in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-empty group and the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv group exhibited a delayed rebound interval (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral load monitoring data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: There was a lower rebounded peak VL (two of three RMs) than pre-ART VL in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv group.
source: Remarkably, there was a lower rebounded peak VL (two of three RMs) than pre-ART VL in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv group, while two of three RMs had a higher rebounded peak VL than pre-ART VL in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-empty group (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral load data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There was significant suppression of total SIV DNA and integrated SIV DNA provirus in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv group.
source: Although there were no obvious viral blips observed in these RMs, we found significant suppression of total SIV DNA and integrated SIV DNA provirus in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv group. However, the copies of the SIV DNA provirus were significantly improved in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-empty group and ART+saline group (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: The Pol-specific SFCs amount on day 70 (511 SFCs/106 PBMCs, post-vaccination) was higher than that on day 33 (315 SFCs/106 PBMCs, pre-vaccination) in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv group.
source: Specifically, the Pol-specific SFCs amount on day 70 (511 SFCs/106 peripheral blood mononuclear cells [PBMCs], post-vaccination) was higher than that on day 33 (315 SFCs/106 PBMCs, pre-vaccination) in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv group.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISpot data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The CD4+/CD8+ T cell ratio after treatment was effectively ameliorated in the RMs of the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv group.
source: In addition, the CD4+/CD8+ T cell ratio (Figure 5H) and body weight (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) after treatment were effectively ameliorated in the RMs of the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv group, but not in the ART+HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-empty group and ART+saline group.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: ICP34.5 is a neurotoxicity factor that can antagonize innate immune responses, including PKR, TANK binding kinase (TBK1) signaling, and Beclin1-mediated apoptosis.
source: ICP34.5 is a neurotoxicity factor that can antagonize innate immune responses, including PKR, TANK binding kinase (TBK1) signaling, and Beclin1-mediated apoptosis (He et al., 1997; Manivanh et al., 2017; Orvedahl et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ICP34.5 binds to host PP1 and mediates the dephosphorylation of eIF2α.
source: ICP34.5 binds to host PP1 and mediates the dephosphorylation of eIF2α, thus allowing protein synthesis and reversing the effects of PKR and host antiviral functions (He et al., 1997; He et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HSF1 could positively regulate HIV gene transcription.
source: Interestingly, previous reports indicated that HSF1 could positively regulate HIV gene transcription (Rawat and Mitra, 2011), which is facilitated by its nuclear entry post-phosphorylation and subsequent recruitment of p300 for self-acetylation, along with binding to the HIV-1 LTR.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: HSF1 could further orchestrate p-TEFb recruitment to promote HIV-1 transcriptional elongation.
source: Studies have also shown that HSF1 could further orchestrate p-TEFb recruitment to promote HIV-1 transcriptional elongation (Peng et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2018; Pan et al., 2016b; Pan et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ICP34.5 could disrupt the NF-κB pathway and possibly affect the maturation of dendritic cells.
source: Consistently, previous studies have also suggested that ICP34.5 could disrupt the NF-κB pathway and possibly affect the maturation of dendritic cells (Jin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: HIV-specific CTLs can facilitate the suppression of latent viral reservoirs.
source: Increasing evidence has indicated that HIV-specific CTLs can facilitate the suppression of latent viral reservoirs, and, thus, the induction of robust and persistent HIV-specific CTL responses is essential for achieving long-term disease-free and transmission-free HIV control (Collins et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Featured polyfunctional CD8+ T cells may contribute to HIV elite controllers or long-term non-progressors.
source: Featured polyfunctional CD8+ T cells may contribute to HIV elite controllers or long-term non-progressors, a rare proportion of HIV-infected individuals who can spontaneously control viral replication even without ART treatment (Owen et al., 2010; Ferre et al., 2009; O'Connell et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Strong antigen-specific CD8+ T cell immune responses, especially effector memory CD8+ T cells, were associated with a lower VL.
source: In addition, both our previous study and others have demonstrated that strong antigen-specific CD8+ T cell immune responses, especially effector memory CD8+ T cells, were associated with a lower VL, and in vivo CD8+ lymphocyte depletion with intravenous infusion of anti-CD8 monoclonal antibody could lead to dramatical viral rebound in these vaccinated elite macaques (Perdomo-Celis et al., 2022; Pandrea et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2010; Pan et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature including the authors' own work.

claim: The ICP47 protein can bind to the transporter associated with antigen presentation (TAP) 1/2, inhibiting the transport of viral peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: The ICP47 protein, encoded by the US12 gene, can bind to the transporter associated with antigen presentation (TAP) 1/2, inhibiting the transport of viral peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum and the loading of peptides onto nascent major histocompatibility complex class I molecules to activate CD8+ T cells (Orr et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PD1 upregulation can result in the exhaustion and dysfunction of CD8+ T cells.
source: Among them, PD1 upregulation can result in the exhaustion and dysfunction of CD8+ T cells (Trautmann et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PD1 expression on memory CD4+ T cells might be linked with HIV latency.
source: In addition, PD1 expression on memory CD4+ T cells might be linked with HIV latency.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv vaccine resulted in delayed viral rebound and a lower peak VL post-rebound than pre-ART treatment but did not completely suppress SIV virus rebound.
source: Second, the HSV-ΔICP34.5ΔICP47-sPD1-SIVgag/SIVenv vaccine resulted in delayed viral rebound and a lower peak VL post-rebound than pre-ART treatment but did not completely suppress SIV virus rebound in this study, which may be attributed to suboptimal doses and treatment, implying that we should further optimize this regimen for eventually achieving an HIV functional cure in future studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the viral load data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The latent HIV proviruses can harbor into the host genome with a quiescent transcription state.
source: The latent HIV proviruses can harbor it into the host genome with a quiescent transcription state, and thus cannot be recognized by immune surveillance or drug killing (Chapman et al., 1991; Pierson et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: During its replication, HSV can activate the double-stranded RNA-dependent protein kinase (PKR) pathway.
source: Indeed, during its replication, HSV can activate the double-stranded RNA-dependent protein kinase (PKR) pathway, and thus phosphorylate the protein translation initiation regulator eIF2α, resulting in the initiation of protein translation (Farassati et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The reactivation potential of HSV might be intertwined with NF-κB, Sp1, and other unknown transcription factors by ICP0, ICP4, and ICP27.
source: Previous studies have shown that the reactivation potential of HSV might be intertwined with NF-κB, Sp1, and other unknown transcription factors by ICP0, ICP4, and ICP27 (Chapman et al., 1991; Amici et al., 2004; Vlach and Pitha, 1992; Mosca et al., 1987b; Golden et al., 1992; Vlach and Pitha, 1993; Mosca et al., 1987a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HSV-ΔICP34.5 exhibited lower virulence and replication ability than wild-type HSV-1.
source: Thus, ICP34.5 deletion is beneficial to improve the safety of HSV-based constructs. As expected, our data have demonstrated experimentally that HSV-ΔICP34.5 exhibited lower virulence and replication ability than wild-type HSV-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under stress-induced conditions, phosphorylation triggers the formation of the HSF1 trimer, thus facilitating its nuclear entry to bind to heat shock elements for gene transcription regulation.
source: Under stress-induced conditions, phosphorylation triggers the formation of the HSF1 trimer, thus facilitating its nuclear entry to bind to heat shock elements for gene transcription regulation (Bonner et al., 2000; Timmons et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HSV-based vaccines expressing HIV/SIV antigen elicited specific CD8+ T cell immune responses in mice and macaques, but the magnitude was not as strong as other viral vectors.
source: Notably, previous studies have shown that HSV-based vaccines expressing HIV/SIV antigen did elicit specific CD8+ T cell immune responses in mice and macaques, but the magnitude was not as strong as other viral vectors (Parker et al., 2007; Murphy et al., 2000; Kaur et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.
